questionsToConsider: What are the three or four problems you actually solve for clients? Each one should become a result.
Which answers mark someone as a strong lead for you: team size, timeline, or asking for a call?
Is a first name and email enough, or does your sales process need a phone number too?
Would you rather collect contact details before the result, or make them optional?
guide.howToUseResponses: Start with anyone who said yes to a call and picked a timeline of this month or the next three months: they are your warmest leads, and their result tells you what to open the conversation with. Group the rest by result and send each group content that matches their problem. Over time, the spread of results shows which service to market hardest.
customizeSteps: Rewrite the four results so each one points to a service or resource you really offer, then match the options on the last question.
Swap the business type and team size options for the segments you sell to, and add a budget question if it helps you qualify.
Share the link from your site, newsletter or social profiles, or embed it on a landing page as your main call to action.

faqs.q: What is a lead generation quiz?
faqs.a: It is a short quiz that gives visitors a useful, personalised result in exchange for their contact details. Because the answers describe their situation, every lead arrives with context your sales team can use.

faqs.q: Should I ask for an email before showing the result?
faqs.a: Asking just before the result works well because people have already invested in the answers. If you want more completions, make the email optional and show the result either way.

faqs.q: How many questions should a lead generation quiz have?
faqs.a: Enough to make the result feel earned, and few enough to finish in a couple of minutes. Seven to ten short questions is a common range.

faqs.q: How does each person get a different result?
faqs.a: The final question routes each answer to its own ending with branching logic, so you can edit the results or add new ones in the builder.

doc.title: Growth check quiz
doc.description: Nine quick questions that end in a tailored growth recommendation.

blocks.title: Where is your growth getting stuck? Answer nine quick questions and you'll get a recommendation for what to fix first.
What kind of business do you run?
How many people work on the business, including you?
Which channels bring you customers today? Pick all that apply.
How steady is the flow of new enquiries from month to month?
Could you say which channel brought in each of your last ten customers?
When do you want to see a change?
Where should we send a copy of your result?
Would a short call to talk through your result be useful?
Last one, and it decides your result. Which of these would you fix first?

options.label: People visit but don't get in touch
Enquiries come in but don't turn into customers
Customers buy once and don't come back

endings.title: Your next step: bring customers back 🔁
endings.bodyMd: A repeat sale is usually easier to win than a new customer. Start with a check-in message a few weeks after purchase and a reason to return, like early access or a reorder reminder.

endings.title: Your next step: get found 🔎
endings.bodyMd: Pick the one channel where your best customers already spend time and show up there every week for a quarter. Steady effort on one channel beats a thin presence on five.

endings.title: Your next step: make it easy to say yes
endings.bodyMd: People are already arriving, so the gap is on the page. Put one clear offer and one way to get in touch near the top, and add proof from real customers right beside it.

endings.title: Your next step: tighten the follow-up
endings.bodyMd: Interest is there, but it cools off. Reply to every enquiry within a working day, and write a simple three-message follow-up so nobody falls through the cracks.
